display.title: The Flax Merchant's Reward: A Story for the Month of Cheshvan
display.summary_short: Why Cheshvan is special, then the story of Reb Eliezer Lipa, a flax merchant who spent his money freeing fellow Jews and was rewarded with two tzaddikim for sons.
display.summary_long: The storyteller explains the month of Cheshvan: why it is called Mar Cheshvan, how Shlomo HaMelech finished the first Beis HaMikdash in Cheshvan but celebrated its dedication in Tishrei, and how Hashem promised that the dedication of the third Beis HaMikdash will be celebrated in Cheshvan. Like the Rambam's scale, one more good deed, especially Ahavas Yisroel, can tip the world. Then comes the story. Reb Eliezer Lipa, a wealthy flax merchant in Poland, used his money to free Jews whom poritzim had jailed for unpaid rent. When his horse wanders off while he dozes, he finds a stranded poritz, drives him to an inn, and overhears the poritz threatening the Jewish innkeeper. Months later he pays the innkeeper's whole debt with the deposit meant for his flax deal, and at the poritz's brother-in-law's estate he refuses to do business until a Jewish boy held hostage is sent home. Both deals still go ahead, and Hashem rewards him with two sons: Rabbi Elimelech of Lizhensk and Rabbi Zusha of Anipoli.
display.lesson: Ahavas Yisroel means giving up something precious, even money or time, to help another Jew; every good deed can tip the scale and bring the Geulah closer.
